triage.name: Selective IgA deficiency
triage.reason: Often asymptomatic but can present with recurrent infections, GI disease or transfusion reactions; diagnosed by immunoglobulin testing.

demographics: More common in people of European ancestry

risk_factors.text: Family history of selective IgA deficiency or another primary immunodeficiency

comorbidities: Autoimmune disease such as celiac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease, or inflammatory bowel disease
family_history: Selective IgA deficiency in a first-degree relative
Common variable immunodeficiency in a relative

chief_complaints.text: I keep getting sinus and ear infections
I've had diarrhea and stomach cramps for months
I feel tired all the time
I had a bad reaction to a blood transfusion

hpi.onset: Often insidious; many people are asymptomatic and found only on lab testing. Symptomatic patients usually describe recurrent infections starting in childhood or early adulthood.
hpi.duration: Lifelong; symptoms may wax and wane over years
hpi.progression: Variable. Some people have no symptoms throughout life; others have recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, or autoimmune disease that can persist or progress.
hpi.location: Depends on the manifestation: sinuses, ears, lungs, or gastrointestinal tract
hpi.quality: Infections are typically purulent and recurrent; GI symptoms are crampy and watery
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for most; severe if bronchiectasis or severe autoimmune disease develops
hpi.timing: Infections often follow a recurrent pattern; GI symptoms may be daily or intermittent
aggravating: Exposure to crowds or sick contacts
pertinent_negatives: Family history of early deaths from infection

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with failure to thrive, recurrent otitis media, or severe respiratory infections; some have no symptoms and are found on screening.
May present with autoimmune disease or malignancy rather than infections; infections may be less prominent.
Usually asymptomatic; may be detected during routine prenatal testing. No specific pregnancy complications are consistently associated.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; often completely asymptomatic
general.moderate: Mildly ill-appearing during an active infection; otherwise comfortable
general.severe: Ill-appearing with recurrent or chronic infection; may look fatigued or chronically unwell
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with severe infection or anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products

labs.caveat: May be elevated when autoimmune disease or chronic infection coexists; normal in asymptomatic patients.
Nonspecific; rises with concurrent infection or autoimmune disease.
Anemia from associated celiac disease, malabsorption, or chronic disease; not caused by the IgA deficiency itself.
Microcytosis suggests iron deficiency from malabsorption or occult GI blood loss.
Low ferritin supports iron deficiency, often from celiac-related malabsorption.
Low B12 can occur with associated autoimmune atrophic gastritis or malabsorption.
Low albumin suggests protein-losing enteropathy or severe malabsorption.
Screen for autoimmune thyroid disease, which is associated with selective IgA deficiency.

confirmatory.why: Shows markedly reduced or absent serum IgA with normal IgG and IgM, confirming selective IgA deficiency

supporting.test: Celiac disease serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA and IgG)
supporting.why: Screens for associated celiac disease; IgG-based testing is needed because IgA-based tests are unreliable when IgA is absent

supporting.test: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with small bowel biopsy
supporting.why: Confirms celiac disease when serology is positive or clinical suspicion is high
supporting.only_if: chronic diarrhea, malabsorption, or positive celiac serology
recurrent pneumonia or chronic productive cough

decision_points: Use IgG-based celiac serology (tTG IgG) because IgA-based tests are unreliable when IgA is absent.
Avoid IgA-containing blood products (e.g., IVIG) due to risk of anaphylaxis from anti-IgA antibodies.
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease and celiac disease.

criteria.name: Selective IgA deficiency diagnostic criteria
criteria.summary: Serum IgA level below 7 mg/dL in a patient older than 4 years, with normal serum IgG and IgM levels, and other causes of low IgA excluded.
items: Exclusion of other causes of hypogammaglobulinemia

differential.name: Common variable immunodeficiency
differential.why_considered: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections with low immunoglobulin levels in an adolescent or adult
differential.trigger: Low IgA plus low IgG or IgM, or infections that worsen over time

history: Infections that are more severe and progressive rather than mild and intermittent
Family history of common variable immunodeficiency
Recurrent pneumonia, bronchiectasis, or chronic sinusitis
exam: Signs of chronic lung disease such as crackles or clubbing
Lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly from granulomatous or lymphoproliferative disease
labs: Low serum IgG in addition to low IgA
Reduced or absent antibody response to vaccines
imaging: Bronchiectasis on high-resolution CT of the chest

differential.name: IgG subclass deficiency
differential.why_considered: Recurrent respiratory infections with normal total immunoglobulin levels

history: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections but normal total IgG
labs: Low level of one or more IgG subclasses (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, or IgG4)

differential.name: Cystic fibrosis
differential.why_considered: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic gastrointestinal symptoms
differential.trigger: Chronic productive cough, nasal polyps, or failure to thrive in a child

history: Chronic productive cough and wheezing from infancy
Steatorrhea, poor weight gain, or failure to thrive
labs: Elevated sweat chloride on sweat testing
imaging: Bronchiectasis and mucus plugging on chest CT

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, bloating, and fatigue, which are also common in selective IgA deficiency

history: Diarrhea with weight loss and bloating triggered by gluten
Symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet
exam: Signs of malabsorption such as pallor or edema
labs: Positive tissue transglutaminase IgA (or IgG if IgA deficient)
Iron deficiency anemia or low ferritin
imaging: Villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia on small bowel biopsy

differential.name: HIV infection
differential.why_considered: Recurrent infections and fatigue in an adult
differential.trigger: Risk factors for HIV acquisition or opportunistic infections

history: Unprotected sex, injection drug use, or other risk factors
Weight loss, night sweats, or opportunistic infections
exam: Oral thrush, generalized lymphadenopathy, or wasting
labs: Positive HIV antibody or antigen test

differential.name: Primary ciliary dyskinesia
differential.why_considered: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic sinusitis

history: Chronic cough and nasal congestion from early childhood
Situs inversus or neonatal respiratory distress
exam: Nasal polyps or chronic otitis media with effusion
labs: Abnormal ciliary beat pattern on biopsy

severity.mild: Asymptomatic or only occasional mild upper respiratory infections; IgA deficiency found incidentally on laboratory testing.
severity.moderate: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections (sinusitis, otitis media, pneumonia) or chronic gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea and bloating, but no chronic lung damage.
severity.severe: Frequent or severe infections, bronchiectasis, or significant autoimmune disease such as celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease.
severity.critical: Anaphylaxis from anti-IgA antibodies after transfusion of IgA-containing blood products, or severe systemic infection.

red_flags.finding: Anaphylaxis during or shortly after a blood transfusion or IVIG infusion
red_flags.meaning: Anti-IgA antibodies reacting to IgA in the blood product; stop the transfusion and treat immediately

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia, or fever during transfusion
red_flags.meaning: Possible severe transfusion reaction; stop the transfusion and evaluate

red_flags.finding: Chronic productive cough with weight loss or night sweats
red_flags.meaning: May indicate bronchiectasis or another chronic lung infection requiring further workup

red_flags.finding: Failure to thrive or recurrent severe infections in a child
red_flags.meaning: May indicate a more severe immunodeficiency than selective IgA deficiency

complications.name: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections
clues: Recurrent sinusitis, otitis media, or pneumonia

complications.name: Autoimmune disease (celiac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease, inflammatory bowel disease)
clues: Chronic diarrhea, weight loss, or bloating
Fatigue, cold intolerance, or weight change

complications.name: Anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products
clues: Hypotension, urticaria, or bronchospasm during transfusion

special_populations.differences: Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally; may present with recurrent otitis media, sinusitis, or failure to thrive. Diagnosis is generally not made before age 4 because IgA levels mature over time.
May present with autoimmune disease or malignancy rather than infections; infections may be less prominent.

Usually asymptomatic; may be detected during routine prenatal testing. No specific pregnancy complications are consistently associated, but anti-IgA antibodies could theoretically affect transfusion management.

key_questions.question: How often do you get sinus, ear, or lung infections, and how many courses of antibiotics have you needed in the past year?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections; frequency and antibiotic use suggest an underlying immunodeficiency

key_questions.question: When did these infections first start?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset in childhood or early adulthood, suggesting a primary immunodeficiency

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea, bloating, or cramping, especially after eating gluten?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic GI symptoms suggesting associated celiac disease

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a reaction to a blood transfusion or an IVIG infusion?
key_questions.looking_for: Anaphylaxis or severe reaction from anti-IgA antibodies against IgA-containing blood products

key_questions.question: Have you been diagnosed with an autoimmune condition such as thyroid disease, celiac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Associated autoimmune disease, which is common with selective IgA deficiency

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had an immunodeficiency, recurrent infections, or an autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency, or autoimmunity

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, weight loss, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a more severe immunodeficiency, malignancy, or chronic infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any opportunistic infections such as oral thrush, Pneumocystis pneumonia, or severe fungal infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a more severe immunodeficiency such as HIV or combined immunodeficiency

key_questions.question: Are you taking any immunosuppressants or medications that affect the immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that could cause secondary hypogammaglobulinemia

key_questions.question: Do you have any allergies, especially to blood products or medications?
key_questions.looking_for: History of transfusion reactions or drug allergies
